Today, teams navigate it through expensive multi-node trial and error, burning GPU-hours on crashes and suboptimal recipes. We present Primus Projection, which closes this loop with two coupled components. First, a hybrid projection engine that measures what it can and simulates what it cannot: GPU microbenchmarks on as few as a single device capture compute kernels and any in-scope communication; a sub-node downscale-measure-upscale workflow analytically restores out-of-scope collectives, FSDP overlap, and the full pipeline schedule at the multi-node target. A pure simulation mode runs entirely on CPU, enabling pre-silicon planning without any GPU. Second, the Primus Tuning Agent treats the projection engine as a fast scoring oracle (seconds per candidate instead of tens of minutes) and uses it to drive an intelligent search over the configuration space. A deterministic seed planner sweeps single axes; an LLM investigation loop proposes cross-axis combinations the planner cannot reach, with an analytic memory pre-filter that rejects infeasible candidates before any GPU time is spent. Validated on Llama 3.1 (dense) and Mixtral 8x22B (MoE) across two GPU generations, all projections stay within ~10% of measured multi-node throughput, and fidelity holds at production scale: 4.7% error on DeepSeek V3 671B at 1,024 GPUs and 1.9% on Qwen3-235B-A22B at 256 GPUs. In a Mixtral 8x22B case study, the Primus Tuning Agent discovers a configuration delivering +27% throughput over the published 4-node BF16 reference at the same scale, in under 30 minutes of single-node exploration.

papers.title: TopicMerge: A Divide and Conquer Approach to Topic Modeling
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in topic modeling have split into two main paths: efficient embedding-based methods that offer scalability but are often outperformed on standard clustering metrics, and Large Language Model (LLM) approaches that achieve state-of-the-art clustering performance but at the cost of prohibitive computational expense and poor scalability. This paper introduces TopicMerge, a novel multi-stage pipeline that bridges these approaches to achieve both state-of-the-art clustering performance and computational efficiency. TopicMerge first employs an efficient clustering pipeline to deliberately over-segment a document corpus into a large set of fine-grained, semantically pure micro-clusters, which are then given initial semantic labels. It then introduces a novel, iterative merging algorithm where an LLM, guided by local neighborhood context, arbitrates on consolidating candidate pairs. These approved merges are then selectively executed and semantically relabeled by the LLM, hierarchically building broader, more coherent topics. Extensive experiments on the Bills and Wiki datasets show that TopicMerge achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance while reducing required LLM calls by over 92% compared to document-level methods, offering a practical and scalable solution.

papers.title: Moment-optimal Gamma approximation of Bessel Process exit times
papers.abstract: We construct finite Gamma convolutions approximating the first hitting time of $1$ by a Bessel process of index $ν>-1$ started at the origin. The scale measure in the classical exponential representation of this law is obtained by squaring the positive half of a dilated modified Lommel polynomial orthogonality measure. Its Jacobi recurrence yields an $N$-factor Gamma convolution that uniquely matches the first $2N$ cumulants, the maximal number attainable in this class. From an exact Gaussian quadrature remainder we derive supergeometric convergence of the Laplace transforms on compact subsets of a common slit plane and geometric convergence of the distribution functions uniformly on the real line. The approximants have total Gamma shape $N(N+ν+1)$, and their Laplace transforms and negative moments decrease to those of the exit law.

papers.title: Program Learning with Verifiable Rewards: Distilling Expert Traces into Programs
papers.abstract: Small language models struggle with tool-use tasks that require following multi-step procedures. Whether these failures reflect limited capability or missing procedural knowledge remains unclear. We introduce Program Learning with Verifiable Rewards (PLVR), which distils expert traces into reusable programs without updating model weights. Frontier models turn recurring operations in the traces into typed primitives and rules, and search assembles them using reference actions and training-task checks. A small frozen model executes the primitives, with deterministic verifiers checking their outputs. The resulting program guides a student's reasoning or checks its proposed actions. We evaluate the same program across students on $τ^2$-Bench Retail and Telecom and LiveMCPBench, using synthetic training tasks and unseen benchmark test tasks. On Telecom, PLVR raises an 8B model's success rate from 43.0% to 91.2%, while larger students reach up to 94.4%, compared with 57.9% for the best baseline. On Retail and LiveMCPBench, PLVR is competitive with the best baselines, although tool search remains more dependent on the student model. These results support program learning as a way to transfer expert procedures across frozen models, trading additional inference computation for more reliable tool use.

papers.title: Plan or Retrieve First? A Scale Study of Tool Discovery Architectures
papers.abstract: Tool-augmented LLM agents discover relevant APIs from large registries before planning execution, yet finite context windows prohibit injecting all tool definitions into a single prompt. The dominant approach, which we term Retrieve-then-Plan (RtP), embeds the user query and retrieves similar tools via approximate nearest-neighbor search. We study an alternative Plan-then-Retrieve (PtR) paradigm in which the LLM first generates Abstract Tool Stubs (hypothesized function signatures describing needed capabilities) which then serve as retrieval queries against the registry. Evaluating on ToolBench (46,984 unique API endpoints, 50 categories) across single-tool (G1), intra-category multi-tool (G2), and cross-category multi-tool (G3) query subsets, we find a clear complexity-dependent crossover: RtP outperforms PtR on single-tool queries while PtR outperforms RtP on multi-tool queries. This crossover holds at every retrieval budget (k=1 to 20), is robust across registry sizes from 1k to 47k APIs, and is consistent across model families (Gemini 2.5 Flash and gpt-oss-120b). We characterize a stub-hallucination failure mode (the LLM invents plausible but non-existent API names) that acts as a double-edged sword: on simple queries PtR's stubs abstract away proper-noun signals that RtP matches directly, yet on complex queries the same mechanism decomposes multi-faceted intent into functional sub-needs. We further analyze token overhead and show that PtR's extra discovery call roughly doubles inference cost, which pays off on multi-tool queries but hurts on single-tool ones, motivating complexity-adaptive routing as a practical direction, one that can be driven by a zero-cost signal already present in the pipeline (RtP's top-1 retrieval score).

papers.title: Structured coordinate systems in $L^p(\mathbb{R})$
papers.abstract: We construct Schauder bases of $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ with significant structural constraints on their elements. For every $1 \leq p< \infty$, we obtain bases of non-negative functions with basis constants arbitrarily close to one, as well as bases with positive biorthogonal functionals. For every $2 \leq p < \infty$, we construct Schauder bases consisting of translates of a single function, which can be chosen to extend to an entire function. When $p>2$, the translation parameters can be chosen from any prescribed unbounded subset of $\mathbb{R}$, a conclusion that fails for $p=2$. Finally, for $p>2$, the entire function generating the basis of translates can also be chosen non-negative.

papers.title: Existence and Uniqueness Proof for the Transport Equation and the Orthogonal Dynamics Equation for Zwanzig's Projection on Gaussian Spaces: A Vanishing Viscosity Method
papers.abstract: We prove the existence of unique solutions ${u\in H^1(0,T;L^2_γ(\mathbb{R}^n))\cap L^2(0,T;H^1_γ(\mathbb{R}^n))}$ of the transport equation $u_t=F\cdot\nabla u+f$ and the orthogonal dynamics equation ${u_t= Q_\text{Z} (F\cdot\nabla) Q_\text{Z} u+f}$, where $F$ is a time-independent vector field, $f$ is a forcing term, $P_\text{Z}=1-Q_\text{Z}$ is a Zwanzig projection (conditional expectation) on $L^2_γ(\mathbb{R}^n)$ defined by $P_\text{Z}h \propto \int h(\cdot ,y) ρ(\cdot,y)\rm{d}y$, and $γ$ is the standard Gaussian measure with density $ρ$. To this end, we develop a vanishing viscosity method based on the maximal regularity theory for the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator on $L^2_γ(\mathbb{R}^n)$. The following assumptions guarantee the existence and uniqueness of strong solutions: ${f\in H^1(0,T;L^2_γ(\mathbb{R}^n))\cap L^2(0,T;H^1_γ(\mathbb{R}^n))}$, ${g\in H^1_γ(\mathbb{R}^n)}$, $F\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^n,\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $\rm{ess\,sup}_{\mathbb{R}^n}\left(x\cdot F-\rm{div}F\right) < \infty$, where $g$ denotes the initial value function.

papers.title: Dynamic Programming for A Linear-Gaussian Dual Control Problem
papers.abstract: We consider an infinite-horizon discounted dynamic programming (DP) problem for a countable-innovation belief-state model. The model is a surrogate for a linear-Gaussian dual control problem involving an unknown parameter vector and Gaussian observation noise. The surrogate preserves the first two moments of the Gaussian innovation and the resulting posterior second-moment structure. We allow unbounded belief and control spaces and nonnegative stage costs with quadratic growth in the posterior mean and covariance. Using a posterior-moment weight, we show that the Bellman operator is a contraction in a weighted sup-norm space. We characterize the optimal cost as the unique solution of the Bellman equation in this space, establish the existence of optimal stationary policies. We further prove weighted sup-norm convergence of value iteration, policy iteration, and optimistic policy iteration under vanishing approximation errors. The convergence results under vanishing approximation errors rely on general weighted sup-norm contraction properties and are applicable beyond the particular dual control problem considered here.

papers.title: The anisotropic Weyl law and Grassmannian equidistribution
papers.abstract: We establish a Weyl law for the codimension-one anisotropic volume spectrum on compact Riemannian manifolds. We then use this law to obtain equidistribution in the full Grassmannian bundle while keeping the ambient metric fixed. More precisely, on every closed connected smooth Riemannian manifold of dimension three through six, we construct smooth, embedded hypersurfaces stationary for anisotropies smoothly converging to area. The cumulative sum of their area measures, when lifted to the Grassmannian bundle, converges to the uniform measure.

papers.title: Autonomous Cyber Operations Gym for Training and Evaluating AI Models for Defence
papers.abstract: This paper proposes an Autonomous Cyber Operations (ACO) gym, a unified framework integrating high-fidelity network emulation, realistic user behaviour modelling for benign network traffic and adversarial profiles, and the generation of cybersecurity scenarios through open toolkits. By supporting live and deferred feature extraction at the packet and flow levels, the gym facilitates the creation of labelled synthetic datasets for training Deep Neural Network (DNN)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs), as well as developing and evaluating modular components for autonomous defence agents through emulated interactions. While evaluation of a DNN classifier within the gym shows high in-domain performance, achieving near-perfect recall on adversarial network flows, our experiments reveal a significant sensitivity to domain shift, showing that even minor changes in network composition, such as variations in traffic protocol distribution, can lead to a catastrophic collapse in model transferability and detection performance.

papers.title: Under what conditions can coupling disorder render qubit dynamics CP-divisible in a finite spin bath?
papers.abstract: We investigate whether unresolved quasi-static Gaussian disorder in system--bath coupling can make finite spin-bath dynamics CP-divisible. The coupling varies between shots but is fixed within each, yielding a disorder-averaged tomographic map. For a single-spin Ising $ZZ$ bath with a fixed initial state, disorder can induce a polarization-dependent transition to CP-divisibility. A bath fully polarized along the longitudinal direction ($|m_z|=1$) yields CP-divisible dynamics irrespective of disorder, whereas zero longitudinal polarization or Haar-sampled bath states fluctuating independently of the coupling between shots preserve CP-indivisibility at any finite disorder strength for nonzero mean coupling. We extend this analytically to inhomogeneous Ising baths of any finite size $N$. For factorized bath preparations, one spin with zero longitudinal polarization and nonzero mean coupling suffices to retain CP-indivisibility at finite disorder. Strong disorder can render partially polarized baths CP-divisible. For homogeneous baths, the critical disorder ratio is independent of $N$. When bath states fluctuate physically between shots, independent Haar sampling preserves CP-indivisibility for finite $N$ if any mean coupling is nonzero. For a single-spin anisotropic Heisenberg bath, any nonzero transverse exchange preserves trace-distance backflow at finite disorder for every fixed preparation, provided the mean coupling is nonzero. Exact diagonalization up to $N=12$ shows trace-distance revivals for a fully polarized bath, in Haar averages over fixed product bath states, and for fluctuating bath states. Transverse exchange and physical bath-state fluctuations with zero average longitudinal polarization preserve CP-indivisibility at finite disorder. Yet increasing disorder can make trace-distance revivals experimentally unresolvable, making the dynamics appear Markovian.

papers.title: Mergers may not be the main channel for galaxy stellar mass growth at redshift $z\gtrsim5$: Predictions from cosmological hierarchical models and simulations
papers.abstract: Mergers are a crucial channel of galaxy growth, but their role relative to star formation remains uncertain at high redshift. Here we investigate merger rates and merger-driven stellar mass assembly for galaxies with stellar mass $M_\star \gtrsim 10^8 \, {\rm M_{\odot}}$ at $z\simeq 5-11$, by combining complementary theoretical approaches within $Λ$CDM. These include the DECODE semi-empirical model, the TNG100 and EAGLE hydrodynamical simulations, and the \textsc{L-Galaxies} semi-analytical model, together with the Millennium and TNG100-Dark simulations used to examine dark matter subhalo statistics and merger timescales. This compares models with different treatments of baryonic physics and galaxy-halo connections. We find that dark matter-only simulations predict merger timescales $\sim 30\%$ longer than those inferred from cosmological simulations including baryons. Galaxy major merger ($M_{\rm \star,sat} / M_{\rm \star,cen} > 0.25$) rates show a substantial model- and mass-dependent redshift evolution. Despite high rates, mergers contribute only $\lesssim 10\%$ to the total cosmic stellar mass density evolution. The average ex-situ stellar mass fraction ranges from a few percent to $\sim 25\%$ for all stellar mass bins at $z\gtrsim 5$, across different models and simulations. Their broad agreement implies that stellar mass assembly at cosmic dawn is dominated by in-situ star formation rather than mergers. These findings suggest that the high pair fractions identified by JWST may not directly trace efficient ex-situ stellar mass growth, highlighting the need for physically motivated merger timescales to interpret galaxy assembly in the early Universe.

papers.title: Cosmic Colliders in Binary Blazars Probing Ultra-High-Energy Particle Physics
papers.abstract: While terrestrial colliders and fixed-target cosmic-ray interactions are bounded at center-of-mass (CM) energies $\sqrt{s} \lesssim \mathcal{O}(10^5)\,\text{GeV}$, we demonstrate that sub-parsec binary blazars form broad-band hadronic ``Cosmic Colliders'', overcoming this limitation. In the compressed overlap region of two nearly aligned jets ($θ_{\rm mis} \sim 1^\circ - 5^\circ$), relativistic proton populations collide at CM energies reaching $\sqrt{s} \sim 10^{10}\,\text{GeV}$ -- six orders of magnitude above the Large Hadron Collider. Operating in an optically thin regime ($τ_{pp} \ll 1$), the system performs a continuous CM energy scan, probing asymptotic QCD scaling, gluon saturation, and Froissart unitarity, while opening a possible high-sensitivity window into physics beyond the Standard Model. Secondary TeV-EeV neutrinos and GeV-TeV $γ$-rays fall within the reach of current and planned observatories such as LHAASO, CTAO, IceCube, and GRAND, establishing binary blazars as laboratories for physics at the ultimate energy limit.

papers.title: Governing Copyright Responsibly in the Era of Generative AI
papers.abstract: Large language models are trained on collections that may include scholarly works, while authors generally lack work-level information about whether and how their works were used. This paper asks how copyright governance frames and operationalises the protection of such authors, and what a responsible alternative would require. Forty legislative, judicial and soft-law instruments issued between 2019 and 2026 were coded deductively against a framework derived from Responsible Research and Innovation theory, yielding 1,337 category assignments across 835 segments. The European Union and the United States are the primary cases; the United Kingdom, China and international bodies serve as comparators. Normative orientation and the distribution of responsibility dominate the corpus, while reflexivity is the least represented category and reaches its minimum in the US sub-corpus. Both primary jurisdictions frame protection procedurally rather than as an entitlement, and no instrument in the corpus creates a general author-facing attribution duty for the use of works in AI training. From the coded gaps, the paper derives a six-instrument governance design and a capacity-based allocation of responsibility among developers, publishers, collecting societies, funders, institutions, regulators, and individual authors.

papers.title: An Integrated Framework for Rule-Based Data Editing
papers.abstract: Statistical data editing in official statistics must restore consistency while limiting changes to observed data. Exact minimum-change correction can be computationally demanding. This paper develops a general framework for structured data whose dependencies admit a normalized acyclic routing representation. It connects routing metadata and explicitly specified semantic edits to logical admissibility, violation diagnosis, and correction. Under stated record semantics, the generated Horn theory characterizes admissibility without materializing its deductive closure. Canonical indices preserve the origin of each requirement and identify the variables that can affect a violation. With complete diagnostics and strictly positive weights, a nonnegative violation Hamiltonian vanishes exactly on admissible records within the specified domain. This characterization is independent of the correction procedure and provides both an objective for correction and a certificate: a verified zero-energy output is admissible and globally minimizes violation energy within its permitted candidate domain. Minimum modification cost is formulated separately, with sufficient conditions for an equivalent penalized objective and optimality certificates based on attained lower bounds. A household survey application illustrates the construction, the verification of admissible corrections, and minimum-cost certification for a subset of outputs. The framework supports traceable validation and correction in official statistics, while statistical accuracy of replacement values requires separate assessment.

papers.title: Geodesic steering for rapid dissipative entanglement distribution
papers.abstract: We describe an optimal-control strategy designed to accelerate the dissipative preparation of complex, highly entangled quantum many-body states. Analogous to optimal steering of isolated quantum systems, our scheme identifies control pulses that guide the evolution of open quantum systems along trajectories of instantaneous steady states while minimizing leakage resulting from non-adiabatic transitions. In many cases of interest, these control parameters can be derived analytically and without the need for computationally expensive numerical simulations of the full many-body master equation. We apply this technique for the preparation of bi- and multipartite entangled states in qubit systems coupled to a common photonic waveguide or a distributed squeezed reservoir. In both scenarios, our optimal-control strategy significantly outperforms the bare relaxation dynamics after a quench, reducing preparation times of near-maximally entangled states by orders of magnitude. This drastic speedup makes dissipative entanglement distribution protocols compatible with high-fidelity quantum information processing applications and illustrates more broadly the potential of leakage minimization for accelerating reservoir-engineering schemes.

papers.title: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models
papers.abstract: Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations---one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks---at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/qlwpc/TG-Interpolation.

papers.title: TheoPhysEval: Assessing AI agents at autonomous theoretical physics problem solving
papers.abstract: We present a suite of 50 unpublished research-level theoretical physics problems with verifiable answers. Without AI assistance, a typical problem in our collection could be solved by a world expert in about a day or less but would take considerably longer for experts in adjacent specialties. We test the ability of off-the-shelf AI agents to tackle these problems autonomously, without human hints. When given access to tools available in a realistic setting, including the ability to search the literature and write scripts for numerical and symbolic work, the best-performing agent, GPT-6-Astra harnessed in Codex, obtains the final answers with a near-perfect accuracy of 98% at an average cost under USD 3 per problem. On average, agents show only small changes in accuracy when denied web search and access to background research papers, suggesting significant memorization of the literature. These results suggest that state-of-the-art agents can accurately perform concrete calculations required across theoretical physics research. We comment on the broader implications of these findings and discuss possible explanations for the current lack of agent-led breakthroughs in theoretical physics despite their outstanding problem-solving abilities.

papers.title: $2$-Large Sets and Nil-Bohr Recurrence: A Disproof of the $2$-Large Is Large Conjecture
papers.abstract: A set $S$ of positive integers is $r$-large if every $r$-coloring of $\mathbb{N}$ contains arbitrarily long monochromatic arithmetic progressions with common difference in $S$. We prove that every $2$-large set is a set of nil-Bohr recurrence, i.e., it meets every nil-Bohr neighborhood of $0$. This proves a conjecture of the first author and gives a sharp answer to a question of Host, Kra, and Maass. Furthermore, we show that a piecewise syndetic set is $2$-large if and only if it is nil-Bohr recurrent. From this, we show that a small modification of a set constructed by the first author is $2$-large but not $3$-large, thereby disproving the $2$-large is large conjecture of Brown, Graham, and Landman. We also deduce that the family of $2$-large sets is not partition regular, thereby answering another question of Brown, Graham, and Landman. We also show that, for every fixed nil-Bohr neighborhood $B$ of $0$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, restricting the common difference to $B$ increases the extremal number for $k$-term arithmetic progressions by at most a factor of $1+\varepsilon$, provided $k$ is sufficiently large.

papers.title: Time-Frequency Continuous-Variable Quantum Teleportation with Single Photons
papers.abstract: Quantum teleportation, a key building block for quantum technologies, enables distant parties, Alice and Bob, to transfer an unknown quantum state using entanglement, local operations, and classical communication. In this work, we propose a quantum teleportation protocol for single-photon time-frequency continuous variables, where time is the time of arrival at a detector. We detail the operational requirements of the protocol, notably the nonlinear interactions needed for the photon-photon time-frequency entangling gate. By explicitly treating the detector position as the reference frame for time of arrival, we show that, even with ideal classical and quantum channels, the input-output fidelity is not unity unless the receiving party can correct the detector-position mismatch. This results in a trade-off between teleportation fidelity and the temporal bandwidth of the input photon wavepacket. The protocol itself can be used for remote detector synchronization. In particular, we show that time-frequency cat and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states provide an internal temporal ruler through fidelity revivals. We further derive the classical and best-copy fidelity thresholds for single-photon Gaussian wavepackets, finding that the relevant vacuum-equivalent shot noise is input-dependent, in contrast with quadrature-based continuous-variable quantum teleportation. Our proposal derives from a quantum theory of space-time events, whereafter we establish space as a reference for the time degree of freedom, thereby grounding our work in ongoing research on reference frames and superselection rules in quantum optics and quantum information. Beyond protocols harnessing time-frequency continuous variables of single photons, this work points toward remote synchronization in quantum communication architectures.

papers.title: Where Polanyi Meets Galois: Tacit Knowing as an Algebro-Deterministic Operation, Toward Re-rooting AI-Generated Science
papers.abstract: Tacit knowing is an operating regime of one memory substrate, not a separate kind of content. In VaCoAl (CASRAM, PyVaCoAl), an algebro-deterministic hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), one DAG of bound records is read in two ways. With every collision repaired (Rescue), the trace is exactly auditable but no path outranks another; with collisions tolerated (Don't Care), a path-integrated confidence $CR_2$ ranks direct over circuitous routes without being stated. This audit-valuation complementarity formalizes Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided. (1) Polanyi's from-to structure reads as non-commutative binding. (2) Full explication destroys the valuation (Lemma 1), as with Polanyi's pianist; tacitness is contingent or regime-bound, placing Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins on one substrate. (3) The same lemma answers the popular dual-process moral ("train slow System 2 to tame fast System 1"), which mirrors the two-store reading of knowledge Polanyi rejected; Mercier and Sperber's reply, that reasoning is intuitive inference about reasons, matches his. (4) To know a large DAG is to cull it. Simon answered Polanyi's Meno argument: a test and a generator suffice. The AlphaGo-to-AlphaProof lineage builds that answer, yet a checker audits an endpoint and values no path: the tacit is relocated, not removed, and results are verified yet rootless. (5) Collins's three tacit knowledges map to bound structure, substrate valuation and value binding. (6) Our mentor-student DAG charts tacit transmission. (7) AI-solved problems with few follow-ups (Tao) are rootless explicit knowledge, re-rooted when LLMs generate, VaCoAl keeps the trace and the community values. (8) On Mercier and Sperber's theory an LLM is a sophist; truth-seeking lies in collective tacit knowing, Polanyi's conviviality, which we conjecture extends beyond humans. Testable predictions follow.

papers.title: Small area learning
papers.abstract: Small area estimation (SAE) traditionally borrows strength across domains through a prespecified working model. We introduce small area learning (SAL), a novel learner-agnostic framework that formulates SAE as a multi-target semi-supervised learning problem and treats outcome prediction as a nuisance task. Areas may differ through unrestricted covariate shift and structured conditional shift, with information shared through common and area-specific components. We develop estimators with and without cross-fitting, accommodating low-complexity and flexible learners and unifying synthetic, model-based, and semi-supervised estimators. For area means, we establish a unified asymptotic theory for these estimator families, characterizing conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality and providing variance estimators and confidence intervals without prescribing a particular learning algorithm. We extend the theory to settings with only aggregated population covariates and characterize the resulting aggregation bias. SAL reveals clearly a bias-variance trade-off: partial residual correction in classical estimators can reduce mean squared error, whereas full correction yields estimators robust to the misspecification of working models, potentially at higher variance. Simulations yield RMSE reductions of 34%-49% relative to direct estimation, with the best configuration varying across settings. The numerical studies also illustrate how shrinkage can produce overly optimistic confidence intervals at the expense of strong modeling assumptions.

papers.title: Uniform-in-Time and Uniform-in-Temperature Particle Approximations of Coulomb MMD Flows
papers.abstract: We study particle approximations of maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) flows with the Coulomb kernel on the torus $\mathbb{T}^d$, $d\ge2$, driven by thermal noise of strength $τ\ge0$. For smooth, strictly positive initial and target densities and i.i.d. initial positions, we prove that the expected Wasserstein-2 distance between the empirical measure and the mean-field solution is at most of order $N^{-1/d}$ for $d\ge3$ and $\sqrt{(\log N)/N}$ for $d=2$, uniformly in time and in the temperature $τ\ge0$, including the deterministic case $τ=0$. At each fixed $τ>0$, we also prove propagation of chaos in total variation for any $k$-fold marginal distributions of particles, uniformly in time, with a bound of order $\sqrt{k/τ}$ times the empirical convergence rate. Our proof uses the modulated free-energy method of Bresch, Jabin, and Wang to reduce the particle convergence estimate to a relaxation estimate that controls the time integral of the mean-field velocity gradient uniformly in $τ\ge0$. Near zero temperature, where the smoothing effect of the noise degenerates, we obtain this estimate by recentering the dynamics at thermal equilibrium and using the damping generated by the Coulomb interaction.

papers.title: BRQGen: Towards Adaptive Completeness Assessment and Follow-Up Question Generation for Bug Reports
papers.abstract: Many bug reports lack the necessary information required to reproduce issues. In early studies, large language models have been employed to generate follow-up questions to enhance incomplete reports. However, they ask a fixed number of questions regardless of whether the report is incomplete. We propose BRQGen, an iterative framework that identifies missing or ambiguous information in bug reports and generates targeted follow-up questions, only if necessary. Reports with no identified gaps are classified as sufficient. When the author responds, BRQGen evaluates whether the answers provide the requested information and generates further questions for any exposed gaps. We curated a novel dataset of 429 incomplete bug reports from Home Assistant and Brave Browser, each containing at least one maintainer follow-up question. Each question is mapped to the author's answer and assigned a label indicating whether the requested information could have been provided directly through the issue template. Earlier maintainer requests were associated with author responses, whereas delayed requests were associated with no response. Among responding authors, requests within one hour received median replies after 0.52 hours in Home Assistant and 1.45 hours in Brave, versus 9.76 and 13.49 hours after four hours. BRQGen covered 35.4% (Qwen 3.8 Flash) to 51.8% (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash) of the 1,073 ground-truth follow-up questions. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash managed to ask 45.7% of all detailed questions and 63.9% of all generic questions. Gemini 3 Flash Preview reached the highest macro-F1 for completeness assessment of 49.3%, but with a post-hoc analysis by getting only the gaps with high severities, Qwen 3.8 Flash reaches 73.6% macro-F1 score. Completeness assessment improved when at least one identified gap had high severity, and nearly all ground-truth questions were captured within the first two iterations.

papers.title: A Circular Cantor Construction Without Dimension Drop for Harmonic Measure
papers.abstract: For every $0<s<1$ we construct a compact $s$-Ahlfors regular set $K\subset\mathbb C$ for which harmonic measure of $\mathbb C\setminus K$ with pole at infinity is comparable to $\mathcal H^s|_K$. In particular, there is no dimension drop for harmonic measure in the domain $\mathbb C\setminus K$. The construction is $N$-adic and based on configurations close to the $N$-th roots of unity. Our construction with corrections to the first order gives the range $0<s<2/3$, while corrections of arbitrary finite order yield the full range $0<s<1$.

papers.title: Solutions of $x_1^2+x_2^2-x_3^2=D$ with small $x_3$: a spectral approach
papers.abstract: We count the integral solutions of $x_1^2+x_2^2-x_3^2=D$ with $|x_3|$ of size at most $M$, for $M$ smaller than $\sqrt D$, using a smooth weight $Φ(x_3/M)$. Such solutions correspond to binary quadratic forms of discriminant $D$, and hence to geodesics in the hyperbolic plane. Under this correspondence, $x_3$ is small exactly when the geodesic passes close to the point $i$. We count these geodesics by the spectral theory of automorphic forms. Throughout, $θ=7/64$ is the Kim-Sarnak exponent. For non-square $D=f^2D_0$, with $D_0$ a fundamental discriminant, the geodesics are closed. We obtain an asymptotic formula with error $O(D^{\varepsilon}f^{1+θ}D_0^{2/3}M^{-1/2})$. The main inputs are the formulas of Duke-Imamoglu-Toth and Baruch-Mao for cycle integrals, the cubic moment bounds of Young and of Andersen-Wu, and a Hecke relation which reduces everything to the fundamental discriminant $D_0$. For $D\equiv 5 \bmod 8$ this counts all solutions, and the range $M\ge D^{1/2-1/1332}$ of Friedlander and Iwaniec improves to $M\ge D^{4/9+\varepsilon}$. For square $D=n^2$ the geodesics run from cusp to cusp, and Hecke theory reduces them to the single geodesic from $0$ to $\infty$. For every $n$ and both parities of $x_3$ we obtain an asymptotic formula with error $O(n^{1+θ+\varepsilon}M^{-1/2})$, which is non-trivial for $M\ge n^{71/96+\varepsilon}$. This improves the range $n^{5/6+\varepsilon}$ of the elementary method and confirms the corrected main term of the author's earlier work. This paper was written in collaboration with Claude (Opus 5.5, High; Fable 5.2 in the final stage), an AI model developed by Anthropic.

papers.title: Sample-Based Quantum Krylov Galerkin Solvers for Elliptic Partial Differential Equations on Curved Geometries with Hardware Validation
papers.abstract: Sample-based quantum solvers measure time-evolved Krylov states and solve the problem classically on the observed basis states. We develop this approach for the positive-definite linear systems of elliptic partial differential equations. A Galerkin solve on the sampled Fourier modes gives the solution. We derive energy-norm error bounds that connect the measured outcome law to the solution error, a sample complexity, and a support-completeness theorem. The theorem shows that time averaging recovers solution modes that are hidden from every selection based on the source. For curved cross sections we give a constructive procedure: conformal coordinates fix the matrix class, isometries of the cross section give postselection rules that keep every solution mode, and the Lie derivative of the metric bounds the error from geometric uncertainty. We apply the method to pulsatile flow in elliptic, lens-shaped, and curved ducts and to non-separable problems with up to 16 qubits. On 16 qubits the sampler reaches 0.2% error with 3% of the Fourier modes, while a selection from the source stalls at 13% error. At these sizes a classical residual-greedy selection is more accurate, but its cost grows with the full dimension, whereas the sampler and the reduced Galerkin solve scale with the number of sampled modes. On IonQ and IBM processors with six and eight qubits, the measured outcome laws follow a replacement-noise model with a common decay of about 0.6% per two-qubit gate, and a parity rule derived from the geometry detects noisy shots at the predicted rate.

papers.title: HarnessNet: Feedback-driven Hierarchical Joint Harness Evolution for Multi-agent Systems
papers.abstract: AI agents can evolve by using environment feedback to revise their harnesses, the software managing model inputs, tool use, memory, and execution, while keeping foundation models frozen. Existing studies focus on single agents, leaving joint harness evolution in multi-agent systems (MAS) underexplored. A single global optimizer faces growing context and workload as the system scales, while access restrictions may prevent sharing agent internals or system-wide feedback. We propose HarnessNet, a framework for hierarchical harness evolution in MAS. Its basic unit, Agentron, comprises an evolvable forward harness, a foundation model, and a local optimizer that can observe and modify only that harness. Agentrons form a layered graph through which environment feedback propagates backward, with upstream optimizers receiving node-specific feedback from the downstream layer. This decomposes joint harness evolution into smaller, coordinated tasks with separate contexts, reducing individual optimizers' context and workload while keeping access local. Optimizers need not access all agent trajectories or raw environment feedback. Experiments on AgentBench with multiple foundation models demonstrate the feasibility of training HarnessNet. Compared with a single global optimizer, HarnessNet achieves comparable performance gains while respecting local privacy and requiring fewer tokens and less time per optimizer call. A migration study shows that the evolved harnesses remain jointly effective after replacing the foundation models, suggesting transferability across models.

papers.title: Uncertainty-aware integration of deuterium metabolic imaging with genome-scale metabolic modeling reveals diet-associated feasible-space remodeling in mouse skeletal muscle
papers.abstract: Deuterium metabolic imaging (DMI) measures glucose-derived labeling in vivo, but noisy time courses complicate network-level interpretation. We developed an uncertainty-aware workflow that integrates dynamic DMI data with genome-scale metabolic modeling (GEM) through soft flux constraints. After injection of [6,6'-2H2]glucose, dynamic spectra were acquired from gastrocnemius, soleus, and tibialis anterior muscles of control and high-fat diet (HFD) mice. A hierarchical four-state kinetic model estimated labeling parameters while accounting for shared plasma input, tissue-specific kinetics, voxel-level fluxes, isotope effects, and measurement uncertainty. Because glucose labeling was more reliable than lactate and glutamate/glutamine signals, only two DMI-derived quantities were used as GEM anchors: glucose processing mapped to hexokinase flux, and glucose-derived oxidative entry mapped to mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase flux. Two-sided soft target intervals with weighted penalties defined DMI-compatible feasible regions for each mouse and muscle. Flux variability analysis and sampling assessed changes across reactions and metabolic subsystems. The constraints were compatible with the muscle network and affected feasible activity in glycolysis, lactate metabolism, pyruvate oxidation, the TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and redox pathways. HFD-associated changes differed by muscle: tibialis anterior and soleus showed reduced glucose-linked feasible activity, whereas gastrocnemius showed mixed changes with preserved or increased TCA and redox activity. This framework connects noninvasive tracer imaging with network-level metabolic inference while avoiding strong claims from poorly identified signals.

papers.title: Plasma-neutral collision operators for hydrogen isotopes: kinetic and gyrokinetic descriptions, comparison to fluid
papers.abstract: Plasma-neutral interactions modify ion and electron velocity distributions, potentially affecting plasma instabilities. In this work we derive ionization, recombination and charge exchange operators for hydrogen-like atoms in a fully kinetic framework, revisiting often-used assumptions of linearity and Maxwellianity, common in usual fluid-based approaches. We first present a comprehensive derivation of plasma-neutral interaction terms in the kinetic and gyrokinetic frameworks. The model naturally retains non-Maxwellian features of both the plasma and neutral distribution functions. By explicitly accounting for velocity-dependent differential cross-sections, the model captures the full kinetic impact of such inelastic collisions on the complete distribution functions of ions and electrons, and not only through their first moments. We include energy losses due to excitation, multi-step ionization and radiative recombination. We show that the fluid moments of the kinetic model reduce to standard fluid source terms under the appropriate assumptions of Maxwellianity and linearity, and specifically discuss deviations from fluid predictions over a range of tokamak-relevant conditions. Substantial discrepancies are observed, even for Maxwellian distributions. For charge exchange, the kinetic model yields momentum and energy exchange rates up to twice those predicted by fluid descriptions. We furthermore show that a fluid treatment of ionization greatly overestimates the mean kinetic energy of the produced electrons. These results pave the way for realistic kinetic interactions between a kinetic or gyrokinetic turbulent plasma and neutrals, particularly in the edge and scrape-off layer.

papers.title: Pro-t-VAE: Closed-Form Student's t Mixtures for Robust Prototype Discovery
papers.abstract: We present a robust deep generative framework for unsupervised image prototype discovery, built on a heavy-tailed Student's t mixture prior, that bridges statistical robustness and mathematical tractability. Existing generative approaches typically rely on noise-prone Gaussian priors or computationally intensive diffusion models; neither simultaneously provides explicit latent structure nor exact analytic optimization. While diffusion models can yield strong priors, iterative sampling and intractable likelihoods limit scalability and interpretability for prototype discovery. We address these issues by constructing a Student's t latent space via a Bayesian scale-mixture formulation. This yields a fully closed-form augmented ELBO for unsupervised Student's t mixture variational autoencoders, which, to our knowledge, is the first such objective applied to robust image prototype discovery, avoiding biased variational approximations and high computational costs in prior heavy-tailed or diffusion-based frameworks. Treating precision as a latent variable automatically modulates each data point's influence, downweighting outliers to learn a data-dependent measure of trust. The result is improved robustness, accuracy, and efficiency, with well-separated latent representations and more stable manifold learning than state-of-the-art methods. We validate our model on standard vision benchmarks and challenging neuroimaging tasks. In brain MRI-driven neurodegenerative disease analysis, our model recovers clean, anatomically coherent prototypes where clinical noise often collapses rare subtypes. These results highlight the ability of our framework to preserve anatomy-associated patterns for precise discovery in clinical settings. Our code is available at: https://github.com/xuzhikangnba/torch-tvae.

papers.title: SPARE: Shared Perception and Adaptive Retrieval of Evidence for Streaming Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires answering questions from the observed video, with evidence drawn from recent observations or earlier events. Historical context can improve recall but may interfere with judgments based on recent frames. Its usefulness depends on both when it is introduced and which clips are selected, while relevance alone does not guarantee sufficient evidence for an answer. We propose SPARE, a framework that combines adaptive historical retrieval with visual encoder sharing. A lightweight gate predicts whether recent observations provide sufficient evidence to answer the question. When additional evidence is predicted to be necessary, a multimodal embedding model retrieves relevant historical clips to supplement the current context. LoRA instruction tuning trains the understanding model to use recent observations and retrieved history jointly and abstain when the evidence remains insufficient. To reduce redundant visual parameters, the understanding and retrieval branches share a visual encoder while retaining separate language backbones. Four linear adapters align the shared features with the retrieval model through distillation at the visual token and final retrieval embedding levels. With visual-only inputs, SPARE achieves 77.78% on the evaluated Real-time and Backward task groups of OVO-Bench and 73.31% on StreamingBench. Compared with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct evaluated at 2 fps, SPARE improves accuracy by 20.68 percentage points on OVO-Bench and 14.15 percentage points on StreamingBench.

papers.title: From almost tight $p$-group enumeration to $2$-group domination among finite groups
papers.abstract: Let $f(n)$ denote the number of isomorphism classes of groups of order $n$. The pioneering works of Higman (\emph{Proc. Lond. Math. Soc.}, 1960) and Sims (\emph{Proc. Lond. Math. Soc.}, 1965), with improvement by Newman and Seeley, establish that \[ \frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac{4}{9}m^2+Ω(m)\leq \log_p f(p^m)\leq \frac{2}{27}m^3+O(m^{5/2}). \] In the same paper in 1965, Sims speculated on improving the error term ($O(m^{8/3})$ at that time) in the upper bound. To show that $f(p^m)\leq \frac{2}{27}m^3+O(m^2)$ is now known as Sims' conjecture. Our first main result proves Sims' conjecture in a strong form as follows: \[ \log_p f(p^m)\leq \frac{2}{27}m^3-\frac{4}{9}m^2+O(m). \] Techniques developed to prove the above lead to progress on some well-known open questions in group enumeration in affirmative, including: (1) 2-group domination in finite group enumeration (Pyber, \emph{Eur. Congr. Math.}, 1996): Let $F(n)$ be the number of groups of order $\leq n$, and $F_2(n)$ be the number of $2$-groups of order $\leq n$. Then \[ \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{F_2(n)}{F(n)} =1. \] (2) A question attributed to Higman and Erdős (see Blackburn--Neumann--Venkataraman, \emph{Cambridge Tracts in Maths.}, 2007) when $m$ is large enough: \[ \text{for } 1<n<2^m, f(n)<f(2^m). \] Our proof refines Sims' enumeration framework using graded Lie brackets, constraints on deeper commutator coordinates, and incidence and Fourier estimates for alternating forms. Normalisation by changes of generating bases then determines the quadratic term in the upper bound. We also prove that all but a $p^{-Ω(m^2)}$ fraction of groups of order $p^m$ have a central elementary abelian Frattini subgroup. The same presentation estimates give fixed-quotient extension bounds which, together with Pyber's prescribed-Sylow theorem and the concentration result, establish domination by $2$-groups of frattini class $2$.

papers.title: Direct Observation of Chirality-Dependent Berry Curvature Dipole via Cross-Axial Nonlinear Hall Effect in Trigonal Te
papers.abstract: Quantum geometric quantities, such as Berry curvature (BC) and quantum metric, are known to govern the physical and topological properties of materials, making access to these quantities critically important for the comprehensive understanding of the materials. Chiral crystals offer a natural platform in which structural handedness can control quantum geometry and nonlinear transport, but direct experimental access to the quantum geometric quantities has remained elusive. Here, we show that trigonal tellurium (Te) hosts an enantiomer-dependent Berry curvature dipole (BCD) that can be accessed through the measurement of cross-axial nonlinear Hall effect (NHE), unlike previously studied in-plane configurations where the BCD contribution vanishes. Angle-resolved measurements on left- and right-handed Te devices reveal a second-order transverse response whose sign reverses with crystal chirality. The extracted cross-axial nonlinear susceptibility, $χ_{yxz}$, exceeds the in-plane susceptibility, $χ_{xxx}$, by more than two-folds, indicating a strong BCD-driven contribution. First-principles calculations attribute this behavior to a topologically nontrivial hedgehog-like BC texture near the H points and predict a BCD that reverses sign between opposite enantiomers, consistent with experiment. These results establish cross-axial nonlinear Hall transport as a symmetry-selective probe of chirality-controlled quantum geometry in tellurium and related chiral materials.

papers.title: A Network Simplex Framework For Discrete Unbalanced Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: The network simplex method is a classical algorithm for minimum cost flow problems formulated as linear programs, that has attracted recent interest from the optimal transport community. Indeed, discrete optimal transport is a subclass of minimum cost flow for which network simplex techniques compute exact solutions while leveraging the inherent problem sparsity. However, extending these approaches to other, nonlinear optimal transport formulations has yet to be thoroughly investigated. In this paper, we adapt the network simplex algorithm to unbalanced optimal transport. Our proposed framework is applicable to various unbalanced formulations, and can be implemented explicitly in the most common cases, including semi-unbalanced optimal transport. The resulting algorithms are memory-efficient, and perform competitively with existing approaches, as shown by our experiments on a range of transport and barycenter calculations.

papers.title: A Simplified Layout Algebra for GPU Kernels
papers.abstract: The layout algebra behind NVIDIA's CuTe library describes how tensor tiles map onto threads and memory. A layout is a shape with a stride for each entry, so a coordinate's address is the sum of its indices times their strides. As formalized by Shah and by Cecka, its central operations (e.g., composition, complement, division, product) are guarded by at least six interacting admissibility conditions. We show that this complexity is an artifact of a representational choice, not of the domain. We present a layout algebra in which every layout names the space its inputs and outputs live in: logical, physical, or thread-value indices. A layout into logical or thread-value space must be a bijection from its $N$ coordinates onto $[0,N)$. A layout into physical space must be alias-free: distinct coordinates land on distinct addresses, except under broadcast, where many threads read one value on purpose and the layout must mark where. Nothing maps out of a physical index. Composing $f$ with $g$ requires only that $f$'s range be exactly $g$'s flattened coordinate set. The index arithmetic can always be emitted naively: compute $f$, split the result by division and remainder into $g$'s coordinates, and apply $g$. Often the composite simplifies to a layout; we show that when it does, there is a coarsest such form, whose digits every other one refines, and we emit that. A warp's or thread's slice is a \emph{restriction}. A restricted layout is no longer composable, which forces the user to settle the whole view of a tile before taking slices. We validate the algebra by reproducing within it CuTe's operations, such as composition, complement, and division. We implement it in OCaml and use the implementation to rederive CuTe's atoms and usage patterns. The decision procedure is proved correct in Rocq.

papers.title: Levy-shaped femtoscopic sources from an exact solution of relativistic hydrodynamics
papers.abstract: An important goal of high-energy physics is to better understand the spacetime structure of particle emitting sources created in heavy-ion collisions. For a fraction of a second, a special form of matter, the so-called quark-gluon plasma (QGP), is created, which can be examined with the toolkit of femtoscopy. With the measurement of correlation functions it was determined that Lévy distributions describe the shape of hadron (pion) emission sources at freeze-out the most accurately; however, based on hydrodynamics Gaussian distributions are typically expected. In this article we showcase an exact solution of the equations of relativistic hydrodynamics, which aims to resolve this puzzle by providing Lévy distributions directly from hydrodynamics. A detailed analysis reveals whether the predictions of this solution are in accordance with observations; in particular, the effective temperatures from angle-averaged transverse mass distributions and the femtoscopic radii from two-particle momentum correlation functions are analyzed.

papers.title: Recovering Irreducible Three-Body Interactions with Lagrangian Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Lagrangian Neural Networks (LNNs) learn mechanical systems from trajectory data by parameterizing a scalar Lagrangian and deriving the dynamics through the Euler-Lagrange equations, biasing the model toward motion that respects the variational structure of mechanics. The interactions studied so far have been pairwise-additive, leaving open whether LNNs can recover an irreducible many-body interaction from motion alone. We address this using the Axilrod-Teller triple-dipole interaction, the leading three-body dispersion term, whose dependence on the collective geometry of three particles cannot be represented by any sum of pairwise terms. We prescribe the kinetic energy exactly and learn only the potential, as a function of interparticle distances and angles. Combined with a signal-aware sampling strategy that concentrates training data where the three-body signal is strongest while preserving broad coverage of configuration space, this recovers the interaction from accelerations alone. The learned potential reproduces the radial scaling, angular dependence, and characteristic sign reversal of the Axilrod-Teller interaction, and generates stable trajectories. Embedding it within a pairwise Lennard-Jones potential lets us examine its observability: the three-body term is recovered once its dynamical signature exceeds the residual modeling error, which it does cleanly at amplified coupling but not at the coupling of a real noble gas, bracketing the transition between the two. Finally, symbolic regression on the trained potential, with no assumed functional form, returns the Axilrod-Teller expression with angular numerator, radial law, and coupling constant intact. An LNN with domain-specific structure can thus recover an irreducible three-body interaction from trajectories as a closed-form law, pointing toward learning interaction laws whose structure is not known a priori.

papers.title: Complexity of Multiblock Convex-Concave Saddle-Point Problems with General Smooth Coupling
papers.abstract: We study multiblock convex--concave saddle-point problems of the form $\min_x\max_y\{f(x)+H(x,y)-g(y)\}$, with separately charged partial-gradient oracles for all three objective components. We impose joint smoothness and strong convexity bounds on the functions $f$ and $g$, together with blockwise Lipschitz conditions on the partial gradients of $H$, so that the resulting oracle complexities reflect the smoothness and dependency parameters specific to each oracle. Under strong convexity, we develop a randomized lifted extragradient method that achieves linear convergence while providing simultaneous complexity guarantees for all oracles. The partial-gradient complexities for $f$ and $g$ exhibit the expected square-root dependence on the corresponding block condition numbers, whereas the coupling-gradient complexities depend on the associated curvature-normalized smoothness parameters. Finite-dimensional bilinear subclasses provide lower-complexity benchmarks within a randomized blockwise linear-span model. When strong convexity of $f$ and $g$ is not assumed, a regularization argument yields expected restricted-gap guarantees with accuracy dependence $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ for the objective-gradient oracles and $\varepsilon^{-1}$ for the coupling-gradient oracles, up to logarithmic factors. Experiments show observed oracle savings and runtime improvements in regimes of poor objective conditioning.

papers.title: Market Impact Estimation via Causal Foundation Models
papers.abstract: When a trader executes a large order, the relevant question is not \emph{what will the price be?} but \emph{what would the price have been had I not traded?} Market impact is thus a causal quantity, yet classical models (Almgren--Chriss, propagators) regress price on flow, which is biased whenever informed flow moves prices through information as well as trading. We present a proof-of-concept \emph{Causal Market Simulator}: a continuous-time causal prior-data fitted network (PFN) trained on a synthetic market prior in which a hidden informational flow confounds the flow--price relation by construction, with confounding strength an exact per-episode knob. On this prior, the naive estimator's bias follows a closed form we confirm empirically (up to 68\% overestimation), while the PFN tracks the unbiased true-parameter oracle at high confounding. Its \emph{do-ablated twin}, the same model with the intervention inputs removed, collapses onto the pre-window mean. Zero-shot, the model responds at the ground-truth scale to metaorders in an ABIDES limit-order book (+0.38 pre-onset standard deviations against seed-replay counterfactuals), and its intervention response replicates on about 2,300 detected flow bursts in BTC/ETH/SOL perpetuals and 3,800 on Nasdaq equities, evidence consistent with, though not proof of, causal transfer. Off-prior the response degrades gracefully, and split-conformal recalibration repairs interval calibration. Transfer hinges on encoding the metaorder as added flow rather than a clamped price level, not on more training. A recurrent state-space variant closes the remaining shape gap: its impact accrues over execution duration where the transformer's stays flat, raising the correlation with measured metaorder impact from +0.68 to between +0.92 and +0.96, at the cost of weaker on-prior deconfounding that traces to the training recipe rather than to recurrence.

papers.title: Beyond Spatio-Temporal Priors: A Generalizable Approach for Dense Correspondence Matching
papers.abstract: Dense correspondence matching has historically been bounded by simplifying spatio-temporal priors, such as smooth motion and rigid geometry. While effective for classical tasks, these assumptions break down in image editing and reference-guided generation (IEG), where transformations can preserve visual identity while breaking physical continuity. To establish identity-preserving correspondence across such transformations, we introduce FreeMatching, a generalizable framework combining generative and semantic foundation representations with heterogeneous supervision from classical datasets, tracked videos, and synthetic scenes. Teacher-guided iterative refinement further improves correspondence in IEG without dense correspondence annotations. Experimentally, a single FreeMatching model substantially improves correspondence quality on challenging IEG image pairs while retaining competitive performance on classical benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate its utility as a quantitative metric for evaluating identity preservation, with scores that correlate with human judgment. The code is available at https://github.com/luping-liu/FreeMatching.

papers.title: Discovery of the Slowest Radio Pulsar in the Small Magellanic Cloud
papers.abstract: We report the discovery of a new radio pulsar PSR J0103$-$72 in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) through a reanalysis of Parkes/Murriyang archival observations targeting supernova remnants and pulsar-wind nebulae in the SMC. Previously two pulsars were discovered in these observations, and PSR J0103$-$72 is the third which we independently detected in two observations of its target field. It has a spin period of 1.327 sec and a dispersion measure (DM) of $272\pm13~\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}}$, making it the slowest known radio pulsar in the SMC with the second-highest DM. We did not identify any plausible supernova remnant or pulsar-wind nebula associated with the pulsar. Subtracting the predicted Galactic foreground leaves a DM contribution of $\sim 230$--$242~\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}}$, which may suggest a long path through the ionized medium of the SMC, enhanced ionized gas along the sightline, or both. Although these data had previously been searched using both FFT and fast folding algorithms, our FFT-based reprocessing found PSR J0103$-$72 through search techniques which have previously been highly effective in discovering a large number of pulsars in other surveys. This discovery shows that candidates with weak Fourier-domain significance can reveal faint, narrow-duty cycle pulsars missed in earlier extragalactic pulsar searches.

papers.title: The Imaginary Component of the Weak Momentum: Spectral Vanishing and Gauge Invariance
papers.abstract: We establish a rigorous functional-analytic framework for the imaginary component $p_I$ of the complex weak momentum $p_Q = p_R + ip_I = \frac{\hbar}{i}\nabla\lnψ$. For every wavefunction in the Sobolev space $H^1(Ω)$, including those with nodal sets, we prove that the expectation value of $p_I$ vanishes identically, as a consequence of the regularity of $ρ= |ψ|^2$ and without appeal to the polar form $ψ= Re^{iS/\hbar}$. We further show that \textnormal{(i)} the Bohm quantum potential arises entirely from $p_I$ and satisfies $\langle V_{\mathrm{qu}}\rangle = \langle p_I^2\rangle/2m$, from which the known Fisher information relation follows as a corollary; \textnormal{(ii)} the group velocity of a Bloch band is the density-weighted average of $p_R/m$, with no contribution from $p_I$; \textnormal{(iii)} the decomposition is gauge-invariant under magnetic minimal coupling, the vector potential acting only on $p_R$; and \textnormal{(iv)} the results extend to curved Riemannian manifolds.

papers.title: Can LLMs Fix It Without Code? Toward Automated Verification of No-Code Bug Fixes
papers.abstract: A no-code fix resolves an invalid bug report by directing the user to change a setting, update to a version where the problem is already fixed, or adjust their workflow. Manually verifying whether a proposed no-code fix resolves the reported bug takes considerable developer time. This study proposes an automated, execution-based pipeline for evaluating the capability of large language models (LLMs) to generate no-code fixes in a real browser environment. We evaluate 322 no-code fixes generated by the 12 configurations released with the benchmark of a previous study, covering bug reports categorized as Faulty Configuration, Wrong Version, or External System & Dependency. An executor agent applies each fix by following its natural-language instructions, and an issue-specific checker determines whether the reported bug persists. We repeat the pipeline with three executors: two Computer-Use Agents, OpenCUA-72B and Claude Sonnet 5, and one multimodal agentic LLM, Meta's Muse Glimmer. Only 17.6% of the candidate issues could be set up and passed both sanity gates. Across the 322 fixes, 14.6% to 49.7% resolved the bug depending on the executor, and the strongest configuration, Claude Opus 4.6 in the Vanilla pipeline, resolved up to 74.1% of its fixes under Claude Sonnet 5. Changing only the executor shifted a configuration's resolution rate by 38.8% on average, and the three executors reached the same verdict on only 46.9% of the fixes. Compared with human execution, the executors matched the human consensus for 66.1% to 88.1% of the sampled fixes. Even under the best executor, fewer than half of the LLM-generated no-code fixes resolve the reported bug, so such fixes need verification before they reach users. Execution-based verification can provide this, but the measured capability depends strongly on the executor, which evaluations must report and control.

papers.title: Idempotence criteria for lazy cellular automata
papers.abstract: A lazy cellular automaton $τ:A^G\to A^G$ is determined by a finite neighborhood $S\subseteq G$ containing the group identity $e$, a pattern $p\in A^S$, and a writing symbol $a\in A\setminus\{p(e)\}$: its local rule is equal to the projection to $e$ except when it reads the pattern $p$, in which case it writes $a$. For a nonempty subset $T$ of the fiber $S_a:= p^{-1}(a)$, we introduce compatibility conditions on $p$ along the right translates $St$, $t\in T$. We show that, over every group, the existence of a compatible set is necessary for $τ$ to be non-idempotent, and that it is also sufficient whenever each element of $S_a$ normalizes the fiber $S_{p(e)}$. In particular, compatibility characterizes non-idempotence over abelian groups, which yields a test using $O(|S|^3)$ elementary operations, instead of an exhaustive search that is exponential in $|S|$. Finally, for every dihedral group $D_n$ with $n\geq 4$, we construct an idempotent lazy cellular automaton that admits a compatible set, showing that the normalization hypothesis cannot simply be dropped.

papers.title: A joint error metric for scoring CFD against wind tunnel data, scaled by the robust spread of the participants (AutoCFD5 Case 2)
papers.abstract: Case 2 of the 5th Automotive CFD Prediction Workshop (AutoCFD5) compares the participants' CFD results with wind tunnel measurements of surface pressure, velocity profiles and force coefficients. To place each run on a diagram of error against computational cost, these quantities must be combined into one number. This note defines that number, the joint error. Following the practice of interlaboratory proficiency testing (ISO 13528), every deviation from the experiment is expressed in units of the spread of the participants' results at that point, estimated robustly with the standard's Algorithm A. The point-wise spreads are pooled into one scale per component, so that every measurement point carries equal weight within its component. Configurations 2a and 2b share these scales and are compared only on the measurements both have, so that their errors can be shown on one diagram. The joint error is a fixed weighted sum of five component errors. The scales are computed once from all AutoCFD5 submissions received by 28 October 2026 and then frozen, so that scores are reproducible and comparable across workshops.

papers.title: Evaluating Local Language Model Agents for Data Engineering: An Empirical Software Engineering Study of Mobility Workflows
papers.abstract: Context: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used as software and data-engineering assistants, yet evidence about locally deployable open-weight agents remains limited. Existing evaluations often emphasise textual responses or isolated code rather than complete engineering artifacts. Objectives: We evaluate whether local LLM agents can produce correct and reliable data-engineering artifacts, isolate the contribution of a closed-loop workspace and of input-structure knowledge, and examine trade-offs in runtime, cost, and failure behaviour. Methods: We introduce a benchmark of fifteen mobility data-engineering tasks with deterministic checkers for the scripts, tables, structured files, figures, and reports they produce. Sixteen configurations from six model families are evaluated in three conditions (chat-only, chat-schema, agent-with-tools) with five repetitions per model, condition, and task, yielding 3,600 scored attempts on a consumer-grade GPU. Results: A 4-billion-parameter model at 4-bit reaches 77.3%, a 9-billion-parameter model 80.0% within about 6.5 GB, and a 12-billion-parameter model from another family 81.3%, against 98.7% for the highest-scoring configuration, which solves 14 of 15 tasks in all five repetitions. Above two billion parameters the workspace loop raises pass rates by 24.0 to 65.3 points over uninformed one-shot generation, and its contribution exceeds that of the input-structure summary in eleven of fifteen tasks. Conclusion: Open-weight models that fit on one consumer GPU support a meaningful share of data-engineering work once given a workspace loop, although capability still separates usable from unusable configurations and high-stakes outputs need validation. Being mobility-specific and checker-based, the benchmark characterizes the evaluated configurations, not all data-engineering practice.

papers.title: SAIL: Scientific Agentic Intelligence via a Science-Aware Loop
papers.abstract: We introduce SAIL, an open model with 35B total and 3B active parameters for literature research, scientific coding, and multi-step research workflows. SAIL is developed through a science-aware improvement loop: agents built on frontier AI models analyze its task failures and construct training tasks that address the underlying capability gaps. The diagnosis examines search and evidence selection in literature tasks, scientific assumptions and reasoning in coding, and planning and revision in longer investigations. The agents draw on paper collections and scientific code repositories to build problems, interaction trajectories, and executable tasks with the required environments and tools. We repeat this loop over multiple development cycles and train SAIL through supervised fine-tuning, specialist training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and agentic reinforcement learning. SAIL achieves competitive performance across scientific research tasks with substantially fewer parameters than leading open-weight models.

papers.title: Stochastic Snowball States in Planetary Climate
papers.abstract: Motivated by the recent finding of Ji and Abbot (2025) that at moderate eccentricity (0.2--0.3) the planetary Snowball bistability vanishes, we have introduced stochasticity of the orbital eccentricity into a simplified version of the energy balance model of Eisenman and Wettlaufer (2009) to study a general Earth-like planet. The stochastic eccentricity is approximated by two dominant time scales, annual and daily, and is introduced through an analysis of the Kepler equation. We find that, apart from mean eccentricities less than 0.1, the stochastic dynamics are quantitatively and qualitatively different than the deterministic dynamics. For a fixed mean eccentricity, fluctuations in eccentricity amplify the asymmetry and intermittency in radiative flux forcing, thereby increasing the time it takes to reach a stable seasonal cycle. As the mean eccentricity increases above 0.1, the stochastic transition from the Snowball to non-Snowball state occurs over a range of mean stellar flux $ΔS^*$ rather that at a particular stellar flux $S^*$ for the deterministic case. Moreover, as the mean eccentricity increases from 0.1 and the variance of the annual eccentricity fluctuations increases, $ΔS^*$ increases and the probability of the system reaching a steady state and experiencing a Snowball to non-Snowball bifurcation decreases. This implies that there may be many high eccentricity planetary systems in a perpetually transient state.

papers.title: Wind-Fed Magnetic Flux and the Emergence of X-ray Coronae in Active Galactic Nuclei
papers.abstract: We propose a scenario for the onset of radiatively efficient Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) in which circumnuclear stellar and supernova-driven winds supply mass and partially ordered magnetic flux to a compact disk reservoir around a supermassive black hole. A coherent poloidal component surviving advection to small radii strengthens inward, lowering the gas plasma beta until mean Maxwell stresses overtake MRI turbulence, compress the disk vertically, and open a magnetically dominated wedge above it. Within a quasi-force-free description of this wedge, the field self-organizes toward a critical twist at which the net radial transport changes sign, defining a magnetic saturation radius $r_c\sim10\,r_g$. The magnetic squeezing of the disk fixes the pressure balance at the interface between the disk and wedge, confining the accumulated flux at $r_c$: flux advected toward this boundary is preferentially shed, fixing $B_r\propto r^{-2}$ in the interior. From the field topology alone we then derive a normalized saturation flux $ϕ\sim 50$, consistent with the MAD plateau of GRMHD simulations. The resulting compact, time-dependent saturation region is a natural candidate for the AGN X-ray corona, being collisionless, magnetized, and, at high compactness, plausibly pair-rich, with hadronic pair injection providing a conditional additional channel. Its size, variability, and spectral hardness are controlled by $r_c$, the compactness, and the magnetization. We connect these scalings to observed coronal sizes, variability, and the power partition between the corona and jet. We further propose that Little Red and Blue Dots could represent a disk-reservoir phase preceding luminous AGN activity.

papers.title: Gluons and Knots
papers.abstract: We argue that the scattering amplitude of a single minus helicity gluon with arbitrarily many positive helicity gluons is topological. The amplitude is constant in chambers of kinematic space, its resonances are located at walls and its factorization is determined by wall-crossing. Yangian invariance dictates the amplitude to be determined by a 2d null Wilson loop that can be lifted into a positive and transverse 3d link. By reinterpreting wall-crossing and the Weinberg soft theorem as skein relations and Reidemeister moves of the subknots, we construct a state-counting description consisting of adding the `corners' of their HOMFLY-PT polynomials. Beyond the classical limit, we argue that this provides a conjectured but precise connection to topological field and string theory. The new formula is rigorously derived via a Lean-formalized dependency graph (DAG) as detailed in a companion paper, laying out the precise assumptions including Reidemeister III invariance. It is further tested exhaustively, including novel `star' kinematics where the amplitude and state count are shown to become Catalan numbers, in agreement with knot theory literature.

papers.title: Coefficient arithmetic and Mellin moments of the Rogers-Ramanujan continued fraction
papers.abstract: We study the signs of logarithmic coefficients associated with the Rogers-Ramanujan continued fraction. An explicit criterion involving a finite product determines whether all coefficients in an arithmetic progression are negative or both signs occur with positive natural density. On the sets $n=5^a m$, $5\nmid m$, negative coefficients occur with positive relative density $δ_a^-$ at every fixed $a$. If $m_a$ is the least such $m$, we prove that both $5^{-a}\log\log(1/δ_a^-)$ and $5^{-a}\log\log m_a$ tend to $5\logϕ/(12e^γ)$, where $ϕ=(1+\sqrt5)/2$ and $γ$ is Euler's constant. These are leading double-logarithmic asymptotics, obtained from classical results on additive and multiplicative functions. Coefficient formulas also give irrationality and nonvanishing, determine the poles and residues of generating functions for normalized Mellin moments, and imply that these generating functions are not D-finite. We conclude with applications to integrals involving zeta, Dirichlet $L$, and cusp-form $L$-functions.

papers.title: EmbodiedRSI: Active Continual Robot Learning Through Hypothesis-Guided Co-Evolution
papers.abstract: Robot foundation models provide strong visuomotor control, yet their performance can degrade when object positions or task instructions change. Further improvements often require post-training on substantial robot data, which can be costly to collect through methods such as teleoperation. Agentic harnesses can adapt around the model, but current self-evolving harnesses use robot trials inefficiently when deciding which code and skill changes to pursue. We introduce EmbodiedRSI, a self-evolving agentic harness that autonomously decides where to explore next and turns the resulting physical interaction into improved code and skills. EmbodiedRSI realizes this through a Fast-Slow Dual-System Architecture, in which competing code and skill hypotheses are maintained in a Hypothesis Graph. Value-of-Information Experiment Selection chooses physical experiments that can distinguish these hypotheses. Their outcomes guide Code-Skill Co-Evolution. The Slow System builds Hierarchical Memory, and Reward-Grounded Memory Learning selects effective memory according to their value for later Fast-System improvement. On RoboCasa365, EmbodiedRSI reaches 77.0% overall success and 71.3% on Composite-Unseen, compared with 40.1% for the best baseline. EmbodiedRSI also reaches 86.8% overall success on LIBERO-Pro. Beyond benchmark performance, EmbodiedRSI transfers zero-shot to real-world robot, achieving 71.3% overall success across multiple challenging tasks.
